#7802. Didn't I See That Guy on All Those Medical TV Shows?

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Plus an interesting discussion of implied facts, and Virginia libel law on the requirement that a statement sufficiently tend to damage reputation.

From Judge Norman Moon (W.D. Va.) Wednesday in Smith v. Rector & Visitors of Univ. of Va.:

The University of Virginia's ("UVA") Post-Baccalaureate Pre-Medical Program is a one-year curriculum designed for pre-med students who did not complete all prerequisites during their undergraduate study…. The Program … boasts a 94% medical-school placement rate and, accordingly, is highly selective ….

Plaintiff … did exceptionally well [in the Program], earning a "near-perfect" GPA and a 96th-percentile score on the Medical College Admission Test …. [After finishing the Program,] Plaintiff applied to thirty medical schools …. Plaintiff asked the [Post-Baccalaureate Pre-Medical Program Committee] for a letter of recommendation. These "Committee Letters" reflect "the Program's collective institutional assessment of the applicant," scaled on a score of 1 (unable to recommend at this time) to 5 (recommended with enthusiasm)…

Plaintiff alleges that he received "highly favorable" letters from his individual recommenders, who praised his intellect, work ethic, personality, and overall potential to succeed in medical school. In contrast to these letters, however, the Committee allegedly wrote a "materially adverse" letter and assigned Plaintiff a score of 2 (recommended with reservations)….

Plaintiff was rejected by all thirty medical schools he applied to, twenty-eight rejecting him without an interview. Given his otherwise strong qualifications, Plaintiff identifies the Committee letter as the clear explanation for this failure. But not only did the letter devastate these thirty applications, Plaintiff maintains—it also "derail[ed] his entire future and eradicate[ed] his chances of pursuing a career in medicine." …

Plaintiff sued for, among other things, defamation, based on these statements from the Committee Letter:

The court held that "Statements 1, 4, and 5 are pure expressions of opinion":

The operative parts of these statements are that Plaintiff, relative to other students, was immature, awkward, and had occasional difficulty following class conversation. It is indeed true, as Plaintiff points out, that the Committee's assessments differ from those of his professors in their individual letters of recommendation. But that only suggests a difference of opinion between the professors and the Committee.

One person, endowed with the gift of gab, might believe an individual to be a poor conversationalist, while another person, more maladroit in nature, might believe that same individual to be perfectly charming. Likewise, someone with a particularly high standard for maturity might conclude that someone is immature where most others would disagree. This is to say that the Statements 1, 4, and 5 are "relative in nature and depend largely upon the [Defendants'] viewpoint." {To the extent that Plaintiff alleges that his level 2 "recommended with reservations" rating was itself defamatory, the Court finds that it is also a pure expression of opinion.}

The court concluded that statements 2 and 3 included factual implications, and thus weren't pure opinion:

It is impossible to separate the negative import of each statement from the assumptions that Plaintiff, in fact, did not "keep[ ] his shadowing assignments" and did not "communicat[e] his intended class absences" at least once, as even a single instance of either might reasonably fail to meet expectations in a "highly selective" program. These assumptions, moreover, are susceptible to empirical proof. That the Committee Letter ultimately phrases each statement as a relative assessment does not negate that, if the factual predicates are false, then the assessment must also be false.

But the court concluded that statement 3 was true, since Plaintiff had "acknowledg[ed] three unexcused absences in a class." And it also concluded that statements 2 and 3 weren't sufficiently damaging to reputation to be defamatory:

Statements that are merely "insulting, offensive, or otherwise inappropriate" are not defamatory. The bar is much higher: "Reputation must be affected to a magnitude sufficient to render one odious, infamous, or ridiculous, or subject to disgrace, shame, scorn, or contempt."

Therefore, and relevant here, negative assessments of a person's professional conduct are rarely defamatory unless they suggest "an unfitness to perform the duties of a job or lack of integrity in the performance of duties." … "[A]llegations of unsatisfactory job performance do not in and of themselves so harm [one's] reputation …." …

Statements 2 and 3 do not plausibly rise to this level. The purpose of the Committee Letter was to "convey[ ] UVA's institutional assessment of Plaintiff's readiness and suitability for medical school," and its general tenor was that Plaintiff possesses the raw intellectual capability but would first "benefit from some maturing years," reflected in its recommendation "with reservations." To concretize the Committee's "reservations," the letter stated that Plaintiff "was not as consistent with keeping his shadowing assignments or communicating his intended class absences as expected."

These statements criticize Plaintiff's communication and consistency regarding his attendance—they do not, for instance, suggest that he was chronically absent or that he abandoned his clinical duties. See, e.g., Fuste v. Riverside Healthcare Ass'n, Inc. (Va. 2003) (a statement suggesting two doctors "'abandoned' their patients and that there were 'concerns about their competence'" was defamatory per se); Fleming v. Moore (Va. 1981) (requiring that a statement be "necessarily hurtful" to a plaintiff's occupational fitness to be defamatory per se). Moreover, and as Plaintiff recognizes, these statements were not offered to suggest that he was wholly unsuited for medical school—they were offered in support of his assessment as capable yet not presently ready for medical school. See Dkt. 32 at 20 ("[The Committee Letter] conveyed that Plaintiff presently lacked the maturity, judgment, and readiness required to enter medical school."); id. ("Read in that context, the Committee was telling medical schools that Plaintiff was not yet fit to begin medical training and should not be admitted during the current application cycle."). While this assessment may have harmed Plaintiff's candidacy in the 2025 application cycle, it did not malign his reputation as to render him "odious, infamous, or ridiculous" or subject him to "disgrace, shame, scorn, or contempt."

Charles Walker Terry and Samantha Rosalie Romano (Byrne Canaan Law) represent defendants.

#7801. 7 Surfaces You Should Never Use Ice Melt On

Avoid damaging salt-sensitive outdoor surfaces with these expert-backed suggestions.

Ice melt salt is an effective option for preventing and removing ice from sidewalks, driveways and stairs, but it isn’t suitable for every surface. Applying ice melt to certain materials can cause significant damage and should be avoided. Ahead, learn which surfaces are most vulnerable to damage from ice melt, why it happens and what safer alternatives you can use to keep outdoor areas free from ice.

Ice melt salt chemically reacts with certain materials, accelerates freeze-thaw cycles and alters surface moisture levels to cause damage. The type of damage will depend on the surface and how it interacts with ice melt.

Ice melt contains rock salt, calcium chloride and/or magnesium chloride to melt ice faster and at lower temperatures. While all melting salt is corrosive and can damage outdoor surfaces, ice melt products can react differently than rock salt alone.

Ice melt seeps deeply into porous cement-based materials. The calcium chloride in ice melt can react with elements of concrete or brick to form calcium oxychloride crystals. As the crystals grow, they generate extreme pressure that can cause cracks, surface spalling and crumbling.

De-icing products accelerate freeze-thaw cycles in porous cement-based surfaces, causing them to break down. “It makes the freezing and thawing cycle more aggressive, which is what causes the surface to break up,” Murphy says.

Though less damaging than rock salt, ice melt can still contribute to deterioration. Calcium chloride and magnesium chloride attract and retain moisture, increasing the potential for freeze-thaw damage.

Conversely, ice melt draws moisture out of organic materials, causing them to dry out. Over time, this moisture loss can lead to warping, cracking, splitting and other forms of deterioration.

Ice melt accelerates metal oxidation to create rust. It can corrode rebar embedded in concrete, potentially causing cracks and structural damage, as well as rusting exposed metal stairs and railings.

It’s best to avoid applying salt to these salt-sensitive surfaces.

“New concrete is the most vulnerable because it takes weeks to fully cure, so salt on the surface will cause the top few millimeters to flake off,” Murphy says. To be safe, avoid salting new concrete for the first season.

“Cracked concrete opens up for water to get inside, and salt in the water will only make that worse because it will freeze and thaw more aggressively,” Murphy says.

All ice melt products will damage hard-scape surfaces due to chemical reactions and freeze-thaw cycles. “If you are using them, use them sparingly and remove them as soon as possible to decrease continuous exposure for your hardscape areas,” Zurcher says.

Natural stone like limestone and flagstone can react to ice melt compounds. The porous surface is vulnerable to damaging freeze-thaw cycles as well.

Harsh de-icers can damage dyed, painted or stamped concrete surfaces by breaking down color pigments.

Metal stairs and railings will rapidly rust when salt is applied to them, so it’s best to avoid it.

Ice melt draws moisture from wood, causing cracking, warping and raised fibers. It also degrades paint and stain and leaves behind chalky white salt stains.

Sand: Sand doesn’t melt ice, but does provide traction to prevent slips.

Wood ash: Instead of throwing away wood ash, use it as a salt alternative to melt ice and also provide improved traction.

Electric mats: Installed before cold weather sets in, electric melting mats warm up and prevent ice from ever forming. These can be very effective on stairs and sidewalks.

Weed torch: Weed torches are handy when you need to melt a lot of ice quickly. Do not use one to melt ice on wood and avoid painted or stained concrete as well.

“The best way to reduce damage from these chemicals is to shovel snow as soon as possible,” Zurcher says, so you can use less of them. Use ice melt sparingly, and only as directed. A handful is enough to treat three square yards. Instead of using ice melt alone, mix a small amount with sand to treat surfaces.

Regular sealing protects cement-based products.  “Reseal every three to five years to make sure no water can get in, salty or not,” Murphy says. Additionally, use chloride-free de-icing products, or those labelled as “concrete-safe”.

Newly poured concrete is the most vulnerable to salt damage, but all concrete surfaces will experience damage with enough prolonged exposure to salt.

It depends on the extent of the damage. Major cracks and breakage mean concrete needs to be removed and repoured, Zurcher says, while surface damage could be skim-coated, with potentially limited results.

Pet-safe products will have similar effects on hardscape areas, Zurcher says, as they still contain salt.

#7800. You Can Now Get a Battery Just for Your Fridge—But Is It Better Than a Generator?

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 20, 2026 7:34 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Power outages are top of mind now more than ever before—and for good reason. One in four households experience a power outage in a year, according to U.S. Census Bureau data, and 70 percent of those reporting outages were without power for 6 hours or more. These longer outages are not only disruptive; they can also be expensive, considering that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration recommends tossing perishable food kept in the refrigerator after just 4 hours without power.

Backup power promises comfort and security, which is why so many homes rely on a portable generator or power station. That category has grown from gas-powered generators to multi-fuel units, portable power stations, and whole-home batteries. The newest member of the family? A fridge backup.

Just in 2026, this new style hard-launched with models from three industry leaders: Bluetti’s Fridge Power, Jackery’s FridgeGuard, and Backup Core by BioLite. And the consumer response has been powerful. Bluetti’s Kickstarter hit 145 percent of its funding goal in 45 days. Jackery debuted as a Costco exclusive in June and expanded its retail distribution after hearing about customers carrying home multiple units. BioLite has released its Backup in two waves already, each selling out in weeks, and is taking orders now for January shipments. Clearly, homeowners want a backup built just for the fridge. Keep reading to learn more about what sets fridge backups apart and when one beats a generator.

Fridge-optimized batteries all share three main hallmarks:

Think of it like a larger version of the uninterruptible power supply (UPS) that you might use in a home office or with a high-end entertainment center to keep your connected electronics running during a brownout or blackout. A UPS in the home office might offer surge protection and enough battery life to run your computer for another 5 minutes so you can safely shut it down; this fridge-optimized backup can keep your most important kitchen appliance on for 15 hours or more.

And while we call them “fridge” backups, the design is actually much more versatile. Plug them in and slip the slim backups easily into any room to keep an important appliance operational for hours: under a bed to power a CPAP machine, behind a bookshelf within cord’s reach of an air purifier, or behind the fish tank to maintain the family pet’s habitat.

Kickstarter backers for the Backup by BioLite—which first debuted in 2024 on the crowdfunding platform—“got it” immediately. “They understood the problem it was solving, and most questions revolved around understanding additional applications and setups beyond the fridge because the kitchen application was so intuitive,” says Erica Rosen, the VP of Marketing at BioLite and Goal Zero brands. “For example, we got a lot of questions about sump pumps and if Backup could run one during an outage.” (Spoiler alert: It can.)

Today, homeowners (and renters!) have many options for backup power, each with its own set of pros and cons.

A standby generator or whole-home battery backup automatically kicks in to keep the essentials—if not the whole home—running during an outage. Each type of backup connects at the electrical panel with a transfer switch. As such, each is a larger investment (read: more expensive) and a permanent installation that requires a licensed electrician. These backups also require forethought about fuel. A standby generator will require a source of liquid propane and/or natural gas, whereas whole-home batteries are often charged from the grid before an event and potentially recharged via solar panels when the grid is down.

A portable gas-powered generator is more affordable than a standby option, but should only be run outdoors, which creates some limitations. For starters, you need to be home to turn a portable generator on and connect to your appliance. Then, you’ll need a long, heavy-duty outdoor-rated extension cord to reach the kitchen. These generators operate loudly, emit exhaust fumes, and require you to store enough fuel to be ready for the worst. Assuming you have a good supply, though, you can keep your appliance(s) powered with minimal interruption using a reliable portable generator.

A power station brings backup power indoors to power multiple electronics and small appliances. Power stations are the closest comparison. They are safe to use indoors or out and feature similar battery capacities. You can find options in the ballpark of 1 to 2 kWh for similar price points. They can, but may not always be, plugged in 100 percent of the time to act as a UPS. And importantly, they’re often too bulky to leave out next to a refrigerator 24/7.

A fridge backup offers instant power backup without a permanent installation. It’s ideal for the consumer who is looking for a user-friendly, set-and-forget setup and a safety net that offers enough power to keep a fridge running for approximately 15 hours while the power is out—longer if additional batteries are connected.

“It’s [designed for] someone who wants peace of mind without having to think too much about backup power. Maybe you live somewhere with frequent storms, or you’ve come home after an outage to find everything in your freezer has spoiled,” says Beau Tyrrel, Product Manager at Jackery. “It’s also useful for renters and those who live in apartments and can’t install a whole-home backup system. All you need is a standard outlet, and you can take it with you when you move.”

The design is appealing in more ways than one, notes Luna Yan, affiliate marketing manager at Bluetti. A fridge backup solves spatial problems that come with more traditional portable power stations: “Traditional backup power systems are often bulky, making them difficult to accommodate in homes with limited space, particularly in kitchens and apartments.”

“When we set out to develop Backup, we knew the world didn’t need another box-format power station. We did a lot of user research and found that there was a meaningful gap between the power stations of the world and expensive whole-home backup solutions, and it was leaving a lot of people out of the resiliency conversation,” Rosen says. “As we explored ways to answer this, it became clear that form factor was going to be a really important element: If we wanted something plugged in permanently to enable automatic performance, it needed to be really easy and it could not take up precious living space.”

It’s especially useful if you’re away when the power goes out and can’t move the fridge’s plug to a generator. Already plugged into the wall from setup, the backup’s stored power will be usable immediately. Each model’s mobile app shows outage alerts, battery level, and power draw from anywhere.

“[A fridge backup is] also useful for renters and those who live in apartments and can’t install a whole-home backup system. All you need is a standard outlet, and you can take it with you when you move.”

There’s a cost to every power outage. One of the biggest concerns for most homeowners is the spoiled food in a refrigerator after 4 hours without power. “Refrigerators are one of the few appliances in your home that needs to run around the clock,” Tyrrel says. “When the power goes out, you could lose hundreds of dollars in groceries.”

A blackout can cost the average American household $117 in spoiled groceries, according to a survey of more than 1,000 Americans by the Texas electric provider Payless Power. One in five homes had it worse, losing more than $200 in groceries during a single outage.

Using that average, we estimate that a $1,000 fridge backup pays for itself after 10 blackouts—potentially sooner in larger households or homes with especially packed fridges and freezers. For an area that experiences one to two extended blackouts in a year, this investment could earn its keep in as soon as 6 years—and these new backups are rated for 10 or more years of use.

“Based on customer feedback, refrigerators are among the most important appliances to keep running during a power outage,” Yan says. And for good reason: “Continuous refrigeration helps protect food, medications, and other temperature-sensitive items.”

If your utility company offers a Time-of-Use (TOU) electricity pricing plan, any of these fridge backups can help you take advantage of the savings. TOU programs charge different supply rates based on when you use electricity, incentivizing customers to use more electricity when overall demand is low by charging less per kilowatt-hour (kWh) used. These “off-peak hours” vary by plan, but typically are overnight and early morning.

For the average homeowner, the main way to save on these plans is to optimize the electricity usage you can schedule: when you charge an electric vehicle, run the dishwasher, and wash or dry a load of laundry. A fridge, of course, runs all day, and an efficient, Energy Star-certified model can use anywhere from 358 kWh for a compact top-freezer unit to 805 kWh per year for a large side-by-side refrigerator. You can’t optimize the always-on appliance without either a whole-home power bank that recharges in an off-peak hour for use during peak times or, now, a fridge backup. In a connected mobile app, users specify the best times to charge (off-peak hours) and discharge (peak hours), effectively shifting the fridge’s grid use to cheaper hours.

Especially now, with rising concern about grid stability and the increasing frequency of natural disaster events that disrupt power, demand for energy backups is high. Each of these energy brands has sold out and replenished stock at least once already this year. So while you may be eager to set up your home with the first available fridge backup, here’s a comprehensive look at unit specs to help find the model best suited to your space and needs.

Bluetti’s fridge backup offers the largest base capacity—nearly double that of Jackery FridgeGuard, and expandable to 8 kWh (second only to BioLite’s 10.5 kWh). Divide the total cost by the capacity, and you’re paying about $470 per kWh, which is the most backup per dollar. One unit can power the typical modern fridge for 21 to 48 hours, and a maximized setup of FridgePower plus three BlueCell battery packs can power your fridge for 4 days. (Run time, of course, depends on the specific refrigerator’s energy consumption and usage conditions.) That makes the slim design even more impressive—though at 43 pounds, it’s a two-person job to wall-mount.

The mobile app provides battery levels, outage status, and charging progress, plus a place to choose among four UPS modes: Standard, PV Priority (which prioritizes solar power), TOU (Time-of-Use), and Custom. It even tracks local weather, alerts you when a storm approaches, and switches to fast charging if needed. An optional magnetic display (sold separately) provides at-a-glance information including percentage charged, energy output, and UPS modes—all without opening your phone.

On paper, the Jackery fridge backup appears to be the unit most specialized for fridge use. It offers up to 15 hours of power in the slimmest profile. One outlet (for the fridge) and a single expansion option make it the least flexible of the three—but if the fridge is all you need, it’s a perfect fit. It’s effective, affordable, lasts up to 16 years, and takes only one person to install the lightweight unit on a wall mount (sold separately). It offers surge protection for your most important household appliance during voltage spikes and enough power to start the fridge.

One distinction Jackery has over its competition is a choice between instant backup UPS and a delayed start. “Your refrigerator’s compressor needs a little time to recover,” Tyrrel explains. “When it stops, refrigerant pressure remains high on one side of the system. Restarting too quickly makes the motor work harder and briefly draw several times its normal current. Delayed Start gives the compressor a short pause before restarting, helping avoid unnecessary strain when power flickers on and off.”

From the moment an outage occurs, Backup Core automatically powers a refrigerator for 15 to 30 hours. At 29 inches long, it’s 5 to 6 inches longer than all of the other units, but rotating it can fit one atop even a fridge and its slim design should still slip behind the appliance on its vertical wall mount.

Given its size and expansion capabilities, it should come as no surprise that Backup Core also includes the most outlets for electronics. Whereas another model includes one or two ports on the unit, the forward-thinking BioLite design provides its own power strip—that’s three more openings for small kitchen appliances or other electronics to easily connect.

BioLite’s Backup Core is a 1.5 kWh solution, similar to its sister brand Goal Zero Yeti 1500 (6th generation). “However, Backup can expand in 1.5kWh increments with the ‘Extend’ model, and chain up to 10.5kWh of localized capacity,” Rosen explains. That’s even more than the combined 8kWh capacity of the Yeti Pro 4000 and Yeti Pro Tank 4000. So while Backup Core is the priciest of the three, it’s also the only one that can grow into something close to a whole-home battery. Think of it less as a fridge backup and more as the first piece of a backup system.

#7797. The Safest Way to Shovel Snow, According to Experts

Avoid injury with these expert-backed snow shoveling safety tips.

With autumn in full swing, it’s time to start thinking about preparing for the looming winter months. If you live in a snow-prone climate, this means getting out the shovels, salt and snowblower before the first flakes fly. Even if you’re not new to shoveling, it’s worth learning how to do it safely, as injuries can occur at any time.

Shoveling may seem simple, but can lead to strains, pulls and cardiac events if not done properly. Ahead, learn expert-backed tips to shovel snow the right (and safe) way with insights from cardiologist Dr. Bradley Serwer.

The safest way to shovel snow is to push it as much as possible and avoid lifting. If you must lift snow to remove it, bend at the knees and lift with your legs instead of your back.

“The most important tool when preparing to shovel snow is good common sense,” Serwer says. “Dress appropriately and consider the risks of the job at hand.”

Dress in layers that allow you to remove or open up a layer of clothing as you warm up to avoid getting overheated. Opt for a moisture wicking base layer, a mid-weight layer and a jacket that is wind-resistant and waterproof. Wear warm, waterproof gloves, a hat, warm socks and thick-soled winter boots. For particularly cold temperatures and high winds, add ski goggles and a balaclava to protect sensitive facial skin.

Consider a quick warm up and stretch session for a safer shoveling session. Get your blood pumping with some light activity like jumping jacks, walking in place or climbing up and down the stairs in your home.  Gently stretch major muscle groups before heading outside.

Snow shovels are not all created equal. For safer shoveling, choose one that is less demanding on your back, joints and heart. Ergonomic shovels feature a curved handle that reduces back strain when lifting. Snow plow shovels are meant to push snow only, not lift it. And battery-powered shovels act like mini-snowblowers to quickly remove snow without any manual input.

Keep your back straight, bend at the knees and use your legs to lift snow for safer shoveling. Keep the loaded shovel close to your body, then, without twisting, turn your body toward the direction you place the snow. If snow is wet or deeper than six inches, remove it in smaller layers, rather than one heavy shovelful.

“It is often underestimated what kind of physical workload is required to shovel a substantial amount of snow,” Serwer says. That’s why it’s important to pace yourself, stop regularly and plan ahead to avoid overexertion. Opt for a slow and steady pace, especially if you’re typically sedentary. Rigorous snow shoveling will quickly lead to overexertion and cardiac strain. Going slow allows you to focus on safe shoveling technique, preventing possible muscle strains and pulls. Stay well-hydrated when shoveling and take regular breaks to allow your heart rate to return to normal and your muscles to recover.

Stop shoveling if you’re experiencing cardiac distress, cold-related conditions, dehydration or back strain.

“Shoveling snow can be a very strenuous activity, placing notable strain on the cardiovascular system,” Serwer says. Know the signs of a heart attack before picking up a shovel, like chest pressure, shortness of breath, nausea and radiating arm pain. Stop immediately if you experience these symptoms and seek medical help. “Hire someone else to shovel, especially if you are at a high cardiac risk,” Serwer says.

Dress in layers and cover exposed skin in freezing temperatures and wind. Even with these efforts, frostbite and hypothermia are real risks. Frostbite begins in extremities like fingers and toes, and exposed facial skin. Early signs include pale, cold skin and prickling or numb sensations. Hypothermia happens when core body temperatures drop too low and begins with clumsiness, foggy thinking, fatigue and intense shivering. Stop immediately and go inside to warm up if you experience these symptoms.

“It is very easy to become dehydrated while working in cold climates,” Serwer says, as the human body suppresses the thirst response and dry winter air pulls additional moisture from our bodies. Notice signs of dehydration like fatigue, dry throat, cracked lips or a headache. “Dehydration is often overlooked, and people don’t replace the fluids as needed,” Serwer adds. Stop and take regular water breaks and continue drinking fluids for the remainder of the day if you notice these signs.

Shoveling puts strain on your spine and back, and can lead to serious, long term injuries like herniated disks, sciatica and lower back strains if you’re not careful. Beyond always lifting with your legs, stop shoveling if you feel the early signs of spine and back strain. These include a dull, aching in your lower back, sharp pain when bending or twisting, muscle cramping or shooting pains.

It is safer to push snow rather than lift it.

Individuals with heart disease, obesity, diabetes and high blood pressure should not shovel snow. Those over 45 years old should also exercise caution.

#7796. Some of Trump's Libel Claims Against N.Y. Times Can Go Forward

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Judge Steven Merryday (M.D. Fla.) yesterday in Trump v. N.Y. Times Co.:

Times v. Sullivan states that the First Amendment "prohibits a public official's recovering damages for a defamatory falsehood relating to his official conduct unless he proves that the statement was made with 'actual malice'—that is, with knowledge that it was false or with reckless disregard of whether it was false or not." … {[N]otwithstanding the ordinary meaning and usage of "actual malice," "allegations of ill-will, improper motive or personal animosity play no role in determining whether a defendant acted with actual malice," which "does not concern ill-will, improper motive, or personal animosity," a conclusion which appears correct, in law if not elsewhere in the English language or in the common understanding. In sum, "actual malice is not about whether the speaker had evil intent or a motive arising from ill-will."} "[F]ailure to investigate before publishing, even when a reasonably prudent person would have done so, is not sufficient to establish reckless disregard[.]" Harte-Hanks Communications v. Connaughton (1989).

[But] "reckless disregard may be found where there are obvious reasons to doubt the veracity of the informant or the accuracy of his report." "Although failure to investigate will not alone support a finding of actual malice, the purposeful avoidance of the truth is in a different category." …

The court concluded that a large set of statements that Trump alleges to be libelous aren't actionable, "for one or more of the many and varied reasons amply and ably explained by the defendants in the motion to dismiss." But it concludes that several statements may be actionable, even given the "actual malice" requirement:

[A]s alleged in the complaint, the book, Lucky Loser, includes these statements: (1) "Donald Trump had received the equivalent of more than $400 million from his father, much of it through fraudulent tax evasion schemes"; (2) "In the language of the tax code, Fred had given his son taxable gifts masquerading as loans, a likely tax fraud that went unnoticed"; (3) "A plan was soon devised to funnel some of Fred's cash to Donald and his three siblings. They would accomplish that goal by adding a sham layer to Fred's business, one designed to evade the gift and estate taxes"; (4) "So the Trumps began submitting the padded bills to request rent increases from state officials. Part of the cost of Donld Trump's off-the-books inheritance would be passed along to this father's middle-income tenants"; (5) "Between the trust funds, the invoice-padding operation, and other devices created to siphon off his father's wealth outside the gift and estate tax system, Donald was already collecting almost $2 million a year from his father companies. His own business failures meant he kept that money tax-free"; and (6) "Donald Trump had faced these moments before, periods when it seemed his failures could not be saved only by aggressive tax maneuvers or not paying his debts". As described in the complaint, the second article includes the statement (7) "Federal, state and local authorities looked into his ties with the Mafia, found violations of money laundering rules and penalized him for skirting stock trade rules."

In these seven instances, the allegations of the complaint quite plausibly and reasonably create an inference that the authors and the publishers knew that these statements, accusing the plaintiff of planning and perpetrating complex crimes and knowingly receiving the proceeds and other benefits of these crimes, were "based on incomplete, minimal information" and that the author and the publisher "realized that a responsible assessment of the Trump family's compliance with tax laws would have required forensic auditing, expert tax and legal advice, and other expensive investigatory tools." Further, the complaint alleges that the authors and the publishers knew that "neither President Trump nor Fred Trump was investigated for, charged with, or convicted of tax fraud …."

In other words, the facts alleged in the complaint create at least a plausible inference that the authors and the publishers knew that no reliable conclusion about violations of the tax laws, including especially the estate and gift tax laws, is possible without reliance on qualified opinion formulated after the necessary factual and legal research and analysis, which they knowingly failed to obtain.

The defendants respond in part to the plaintiff's claims based on allegations of crime as follows:

Craig and Buettner "analyz[ed] about one hundred thousand pages of audited financial statements, tax returns, bank records, general records, and legal papers." Their conclusions regarding tax fraud were informed by numerous experts. The 2018 Article quotes Lee-Ford Tritt, an "expert in gift and estate tax law," who said the Trumps' use of All County was "highly suspicious" and could constitute criminal tax fraud; Adam S. Kaufmann, "a former chief of investigations for the Manhattan district attorney's office," who said it "smells like a crime"; and Mitchell Gans, a tax law professor, who explained how gift tax returns can evade IRS scrutiny. Reliance on experts controverts actual malice—particularly when, as here, Plaintiff makes no effort to challenge such reliance. See, e.g., Levan v. Cap. Cities/ABC, Inc. (11th Cir. 1999) (reliance on "numerous objective experts" and "industry professionals" defeated actual malice); Silvester v. Am. Broad. Cos., Inc. (11th Cir. 1988) (no actual malice where challenged publication "was thoroughly researched through interviews with experts").

In response to a question about the basis for the accusation of tax crimes, the defendants identified page 451 in the "Acknowledgements" section of the book, which states, "In coming to terms with the highly technical areas of tax law, we would have been lost in the weeds without the generous help of several experts. We hold a special place in our hearts for Jim Ledley, one of the most prominent estate and trust lawyers in New York, who was endlessly patient and exceptionally generous with his time. Jim made the arcane work fun."

Obviously, even a qualified expert's offering a superficial characterization such as a transaction is "suspicious" or "could" violate the law or attributing to a transaction the (unspecified and undefined) "smell" of crime or noting that a gift tax return can evade IRS scrutiny or generously giving his immensely valuable time to aid laypersons "lost in the weeds" is far from a formal legal opinion sufficient to remove serious doubt about the truthfulness and accuracy of a statement accusing a specific person of fraud or tax evasion or some related crime arising from a specific transaction, including a crime allegedly effected through "ties to the Mafia." The confident detection of tax and other crimes, including money laundering, of the kind that some of the challenged statements attribute to the plaintiff, that is, tax crimes including estate and gift tax crimes and the like, is a task that is intensely fact-dependent, and the law that governs is singularly complex and within the immediate competence of only a relatively small cohort of specialized practitioners.

Anyone who publishes the claim that someone else has committed a crime of the complex nature described in some of the challenged statements and who has not received an explicit opinion from a qualified source after a thorough examination of pertinent facts necessarily proceeds with particularized reason to doubt the truth of their statements and with knowledge of a high degree of probable falsity of the statements; in other words, they know that they don't know, but they are undeterred. Knowing of the necessity for that opinion but failing to procure that opinion is a fine example of the purposeful avoidance of the truth, a knowing failure that remains actionable, even after Times v. Sullivan….

We selected and tested a diverse assortment of waterproof gloves designed for a variety of uses in different seasons. For all of them, our key testing consideration was whether the gloves were truly waterproof. To find out, we used three testing methods and allowed the gloves to thoroughly dry between tests. All comments about sizing are subjective, based on sizing guides provided by the manufacturers and perceived comfort by the tester. On those gloves not listed as unisex, women tested women’s gloves, and men tested men’s gloves.

First, we simulated storm conditions with a rain-wand attachment on a garden hose. The testers wore each pair of gloves beneath a steady 2-minute shower, flexing their hands and turning them over to expose all parts of the gloves to the stream. In the second test, we immersed our gloved hands into a bucket of water, again flexing and rotating to ensure that they were completely wet. Finally, we tested them for wet-gripping ability while handling smooth wet stones. To merit inclusion in this guide, each pair of gloves passed all three tests with minimal water intrusion to the inside of the glove.

Before shopping for the best waterproof gloves, consider the type of work planned for the gloves as well as the kind of materials and construction desired. In this section, we review some key considerations to keep in mind while shopping for the best waterproof gloves, including materials, use, fit, and more.

Choosing the best waterproof gloves depends on how they’ll be used. Work gloves are completely different from those intended for outdoor sports or casual wear.

On garments labeled “waterproof,” the outer shell is usually where the magic happens. Materials like tightly woven nylon, polyester, softshell technical materials, treated leather, and others work well to shed water before it can seep through to the lining. Keep in mind that it’s very rare for leather gloves to actually be waterproof; more likely, they are simply water-resistant.

Aside from shell material, other elements in waterproof gloves’ exteriors make them useful in wet or messy situations. Some of the best waterproof gloves, for example, have textured grips that make it easier for the wearer to grab on to wet, slippery surfaces, making them ideal for skiing, cycling, and other active pursuits. Those looking for waterproof gloves for work may want to invest in gloves with reinforced palms and thumbs, which should last longer and stand up to more wear.

The best waterproof gloves contain an optional outer shell with conductors that transfer the electrical charge from a finger to a touch screen, allowing users to manipulate their phones without removing their gloves.

Some of the best waterproof gloves contain insulation that captures body heat, which forms air pockets that warm with the heat from the hand. Most insulation is a man-made poly-fill material such as Thinsulate or 3M.

To ensure gloves keep warm air inside and cold air from seeping in, some waterproof gloves have long elastic cuffs that hug tight to the wrist and arm, closing off any pathway for air to enter. For even warmer gloves, look for removable liners that can slip inside a waterproof glove to add another layer of insulation.

When selecting the best waterproof gloves, fit and comfort are essential. However, a “good fit” is relative to the activity. A pair of running gloves fits quite differently than a pair of winter work gloves or ski gloves.

Waterproof running or hiking gloves often feel like a stretchy, flexible second skin. Because they’re lightweight and wick away moisture, users sometimes forget they’re even wearing them.

Waterproof work gloves are bulkier and a bit stiff because they’re generally made from thick nylon or leather that resists ripping, tearing, and friction. Moreover, extra padding or reinforcement on the thumbs or palms can add to their bulk. Though work gloves fit loosely, they shouldn’t be so loose that it’s difficult to pick up small items while wearing them.

Ski gloves are flexible but don’t wear particularly well because they’re typically made from materials like nylon. Properly fitting ski gloves fit snugly around the wrist but are roomy enough to allow the skier to manipulate straps on ski poles and boot bindings.

Also consider breathability. If hands sweat and moisture collects inside the glove, it won’t matter that the shell is waterproof because hands will still get wet. Breathable gloves help some of the heat and moisture escape without letting in cold outer air and moisture.

Now that you know a bit more about the factors to consider when choosing the best waterproof gloves for your needs, some questions may remain. The following are some of the most frequently asked questions about the best waterproof gloves, so check for an answer to your question below.

Waterproof means that absolutely no water makes its way into the glove. Water-resistant means that the gloves shed water to a degree before water comes in.

As one of the best options for the warmest waterproof gloves, the Carhartt Cold Snap waterproof gloves are warm enough to protect your hands in very cold temperatures.

You can wash some waterproof gloves, but it’s best to spot clean them and use a boot dryer with a glove attachment if they become soiled.

The best way to dry the inside of waterproof gloves is to put them on a boot dryer with a glove attachment.

#7794. What Actually Happens When Semi-Trucks Stop at Weigh Stations?

Those roadside scales do more than weigh semitrucks. Here’s what inspectors check and what happens when a truck pulls into a weigh station.

Drivers pass truck weigh stations all the time, but few know everything these stations do or what happens when a truck pulls in. Once a semitruck exits and rejoins the highway, it’s hard to tell what goes on in between.

Learn what happens when a truck pulls in, what inspectors look for, and why some drivers can keep going.

Truck weigh stations help states enforce weight limits and spot safety problems. Trucks can weigh too much overall or carry too much weight on certain axles, putting extra strain on roads and bridges. On the Interstate System, the standard federal limits are 80,000 pounds gross vehicle weight, 20,000 pounds on a single axle, and 34,000 pounds on a tandem axle. Federal bridge weight rules and certain exceptions can also affect how much a truck may legally carry. Limits on other roads can vary.

Rules vary by state. “Some require all commercial motor vehicles to stop, while others require only those above a certain weight to stop,” according to the Federal Highway Administration. “Ultimately, States must certify that they are enforcing their weight limits on certain highways in order not to jeopardize their receipt of Federal highway funds.”

Drivers who pull in follow signs directing them to a scale, where their trucks are weighed either while moving slowly or at a complete stop. If the weight is within the limits, they may be cleared to leave. Inspectors may still pull a truck aside for a closer look even when its weight is fine, based on screening results, visible defects, or random selection. An overweight truck may also be inspected further.

Inspectors may check a truck’s tires, brakes, lights, and cargo, along with the driver’s records. They may also review credentials and permits, such as registration and fuel-tax paperwork, along with the driver’s hours-of-service logs. “There are eight levels of inspections ranging from the Level I Inspection, which evaluates both the driver and vehicle, to inspection levels with a more specific area of focus, such as Level VI for radioactive materials and Level VIII for electronic inspections,” according to the Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance.

Drivers of overweight trucks may receive a citation or have to move or remove some cargo before leaving. The exact consequences vary by state and violation.

More serious safety problems, like faulty brakes, can put a truck or driver out of service. A truck placed out of service can’t return to the road until the problem is fixed. Drivers placed out of service must wait until their restrictions end.

Some trucks can skip the stop altogether through electronic bypass programs. These programs use safety records and other information to determine whether a driver can continue without entering the station. Drivers still have to follow any signs or signals telling them to stop.

#7793. Crucial Snow Blower Maintenance Tasks to Complete Before the First Snow

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 21, 2026 10:00 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Imagine your frustration when your driveway is covered in snow after the first winter storm, but your snow blower won’t start. As winter approaches, it’s time to make sure your snow blower is ready to tackle that first snowfall. You’ll want to take a few steps to check that it’s tuned up and ready to go without a hitch. We spoke to Sean Dwyer, senior product manager for commercial and residential wheeled products at Husqvarna Group North America to identify the top snow blower maintenance tasks to prioritize so you are prepared when the first snowflake falls.

By far the most important step is to make sure you have a fresh supply of fuel, says Dwyer. “If you have regular pump fuel, it should be less than 30 days old, and ideally premium grade that’s a non-ethanol blend,” he explains. Fuel can go stale over time and gum up the snow blower’s carburetor. Dwyer recommends running the unit out of gas before storing it. “Otherwise, at a minimum, purchase stabilized canned fuel or add a fuel stabilizer.” Gasoline with a stabilizer typically lasts for about 4 to 6 months.

Spend some time reviewing the key components of the unit. “This means checking engine oil and tire pressures, and also starting the unit to ensure proper wheel drive and auger operation,” notes Dwyer. “This is also a good time to shut the fuel off and run the carburetor dry to give your snow blower the best chance of a successful operation when you need it.”

In addition, pay attention to these additional parts of the snow blower:

Featuring an easy-to-pour package and effective formula, this motor oil washes dirt and deposits out of the engine as it passes through.

Battery-powered snow blowers are convenient, but it’s important to recognize that cold weather and batteries don’t typically work well together, warns Dwyer. Checking battery health is part of regular snow blower maintenance. Rechargeable batteries can degrade over time, and won’t be able to hold as much charge as they age as they do when new. He recommends keeping fully charged batteries in the house or a location where they will remain above freezing temperatures. “If everything is in the cold garage, there is a good chance they won’t work when you need them to,” he explains. “Also, remember that when you are done, bring the batteries back to a warm place so they are ready to go next time.”

Snow blowers typically contain shear bolts (also called pins) as a safety feature. The shear bolts are designed to break to protect the auger gears from damage if the unit runs into hard objects like ice from a blizzard. There is typically one pin on each auger and one or two on the impeller.

To change these components, wear protective gloves. “With the engine shut off, try to rotate each individual auger by hand,” says Dwyer. “You should not be able to rotate the augers, and the shear bolts will be visually present.” To check the impeller, look for the shear bolts, or hold one of the augers firmly, and slowly try to turn the impeller. “Be careful when checking the impeller, as it is tied to the shaft that will drive the augers.”

If these items spin freely, the shear bolt is likely damaged or missing, says Dwyer. Replace any missing or broken bolts to protect your snow blower. It’s a good idea to always keep a stash of shear bolts on hand.

Designed to wear down with use, skid shoes help keep a snow blower’s housing at the correct height and also protect your pavement. They are located on the lower sides of the auger housing and are designed to hold the scraper, located at the bottom of the auger housing, just above the ground, says Dwyer. “As these shoes wear, the scraper will contact the ground and wear will increase,” he explains.

“A simple way to adjust the shoes is to sit the snow blower scraper on something around ¼ inch thick, like a paint stir stick, and then loosen the bolts holding the shoes to adjust them down to contact the ground and retighten,” suggests Dwyer.

#7789. You Can Actually Repair a House in GTA6—But How Realistic Is It?

GTA6 let's you take a break from a life of crime to make some much-needed home repairs on Jason and Lucia's house.

Just in case your algorithm is different from mine, here’s some news: Grand Theft Auto 6 officially released today. After 13 years of waiting, fans of the open-world action-adventure video game series can finally dive into a new, richly detailed and fully realized virtual world. Boot up the game, and you’ll find yourself faced with surprising realism, a world of crime, and the ability to do just about whatever you want. That’s right, even… DIY home improvement jobs?

And it’s not just a short cutscene where you see the house magically go from disrepair to fully fixed up. You, as the player, have to actually do the work, whether you’re drywalling, painting, or roofing. Luckily, it’s just a video game because the game is also set in a fictional version of Florida in the summer, which is probably one of the last places on earth you’d want to be stuck doing any sort of construction work.

Let’s take a look at a few of the home improvement jobs done by GTA6‘s Jason Duval and see if his work meets Family Handyman’s standards.

With his lady friend Lucia on the way back from prison, Jason decides to fix up the place… including the unfinished framing in the center of his living room. Luckily, Jason knows how to hang drywall. The gameplay represents the job pretty accurately— Jason holds the drywall in place and screws it into the studs with an impact driver. We don’t get to see any taping or mudding, though. 7/10

Next, we’ll inspect whether Jason should perhaps prioritize a career as a painter over his life of crime. The painting section is also pretty accurate to the average DIY painting experience. Jason has to choose between three different color options before pouring the paint into a tray and using a roller to paint the wall. It’s pretty boring, which is honestly just like painting in real life — so bonus points for immersive realism. 8/10

One of the first things Jason knows he has to fix before Lucia arrives is the massive hole in his roof that’s letting in a near-constant drip of rain. Luckily, like a lot of DIYers, he has some roofing experience, a cordless nail gun and a stack of shingles just lying around for some reason. Again, this section is pretty realistic. If gamers want the full Florida roofing experience, though, they’ll have to crank their heaters to maximum or perhaps play the game in a sauna. 6/10

Look, I get it. The Grand Theft Auto series is about living out fantasies, providing gamers a sandbox where they can virtually experience the impossible.

But still… “House repairs complete” is a bridge too far. Ask any DIYer, and they will tell you no house is ever fully repaired. Pretending home improvement work could ever be finished is just not realistic and really took me out of the experience. 3/10.

Overall, the game is cool. But to be honest, I’m not sure what the point is now that the house repairs are complete.

#7786. No Pseudonymity for Man Suing Trump+Rubio+Musk over Ukraine-Related Actions

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Chief Judge James Boasberg (D.C.C.) today in Doe v. Trump:

Plaintiff Michael Doe is an American citizen whose wife and daughter reside in Kyiv, Ukraine. In March 2025, his wife and daughter were almost killed in a drone strike. On behalf of himself and a class of Ukrainian refugees, Doe sues President Trump, Secretary Rubio, and Elon Musk for violating, inter alia, a federal statute that imposes sanctions on Russia, the Take Care Clause, and the First Amendment. [The claims are apparently related to the Trump Administration's actions related to sanctions on Russia Musk's actions related to Ukraine and Starlink. -EV]

Generally, a complaint must identify the plaintiffs. That requirement reflects the "presumption in favor of disclosure [of litigants' identities], which stems from the 'general public interest in the openness of governmental processes,' and, more specifically, from the tradition of open judicial proceedings." A party moving to proceed pseudonymously thus "bears the weighty burden of both demonstrating a concrete need for such secrecy[] and identifying the consequences that would likely befall it if forced to proceed in its own name." …

Plaintiff has not established that his interest in pseudonymity outweighs the public's interest in learning his identity….

The Court does not doubt that individuals in Kyiv face brutal, life-threatening dangers, nor does it take their—or their families'—concerns about safety lightly. Plaintiff has failed, however, to link those legitimate fears to his being publicly named in this lawsuit. He provides no evidence that Russia's extensive bombing campaign targets the family members of individuals engaged in Russian-sanction-related lawsuits in the United States. At most, he asserts that "[t]he Russian government have a proven documented history and pattern of targeting anyone, anywhere in the world, who challenges their authority of government," including "documented attempted assassinations" and "the use of sophisticated hacking groups to steal identities, digital assets[,] and to launch drone bombing attacks inside Ukraine."

Doe's broad assertion that Russian retaliates against critics does not establish that it will assassinate him, steal his identity or digital assets, or launch drone strikes at his family members in Ukraine in response to a lawsuit. Absent any specific threats or evidence that his family members will be so targeted, this factor weighs against pseudonymity….

A judge in Michigan was found guilty Monday of drunk driving after he rear-ended a public transit bus, but a district court judge ruled that prosecutors failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that his blood alcohol level met the state’s threshold for intoxication. (Image from Shutterstock)

A judge in Michigan was found guilty Monday of drunk driving after he rear-ended a public transit bus, but a district court judge ruled that prosecutors failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that his blood alcohol level met the threshold for the state’s original charge of a more serious offense.

Warren 37th District Court Chief Judge John M. Chmura, 63, was found guilty of intoxication while driving his Ford Fusion into a parked bus that was displaying hazard lights March 25. But the court rejected the charge of Chmura driving with an elevated high blood alcohol content of 0.17 or greater, according to coverage on Law360.

Novi 52nd District Court Judge David Law noted that Chmura’s judgment had been affected, but he questioned the blood alcohol concentration at the time of the crash.

“This court may think it knows the answer to whether or not this was a high BAC case,” Law said. “But thinking it knows is not enough. It needs to be proven beyond a reasonable doubt.”

A bus driver sitting inside the bus waiting to resume his route was uninjured in the crash. Sterling Heights, Michigan, police officer Jonathan Journeau testified that Chmura smelled of alcohol, slurred his speech and couldn’t maintain his balance.

Chmura’s attorney, David J. Kramer of the David J. Kramer Law Firm, argued that prosecutors could not establish the higher offense because Journeau failed to determine when the judge’s final alcoholic beverage was consumed.

#7783. The sometimes straightforward, sometimes befuddling certiorari process

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

One of the Supreme Court’s most critical functions is deciding what cases to decide.

This process has been explained before, but – given the court is now choosing what cases to hear next term – I’d like to use this column to examine some questions about the certiorari or “cert.” process, as it is known. As we shall see, some of these questions have answers; others do not.

First, a review of the basics. The vast majority of cases come to the Supreme Court in the form of petitions for certiorari, a Latin term meaning “to be more fully informed.” The court receives nearly 4,000 petitions each term and grants review to about 60. By a 100-year-old tradition, review is granted when four of the nine justices want to hear a case. When this occurs, the parties file briefs and the justices hear oral argument before issuing their decision.

This process is a blend of transparent argument and secretive deliberation. The transparent portion is that the losing party in a lower court, the petitioner, files a public petition for certiorari, making the best case for why the court should resolve the legal issue in the case. The winner in the lower court, the respondent, also spells out why the court does not need to review the ruling of the lower court. After that, however, the case disappears into the halls and procedures of the high court.

Question one: how does the court handle and process the petitions?

As noted, by 100-year-old custom, it takes four votes for the court to agree to review a case (the “rule of four”). But the vote to grant or deny cert. is not public. We do not know if a petition met with overwhelming consensus that review was necessary or not, or whether it scraped by or just missed out on being granted.

Nor do we know why the court declines to review a case. When the court agrees to decide a case, the final opinion is likely to make clear why the justices were interested. Denials of cert. petitions, however, are not accompanied by any explanation, except in the few instances when an individual justice writes a dissent from the denial of a petition. Justice Sonia Sotomayor, for example, sometimes points out in a dissent or concurrence what she deems to be an important issue of individual rights in criminal cases. But such dissents are relatively infrequent.

This can be frustrating to counsel: Just how much interest an unsuccessful petition attracted would be useful to lawyers trying to decide whether to petition the court in the future on an issue that has been turned down one or more times.

Question two: what roles do the law clerks and justices play?

The answer is known to some extent but secret in other respects. For seven of the nine justices – all but Justices Samuel Alito and Neil Gorsuch – the initial review is by a single law clerk who writes a memo to be shared with the seven justices who participate in a “pool” for reviewing the petitions. Clerks to Alito and Gorsuch handle the petitions on their own.

But much about this aspect of the process remains hidden from public view. Little is known outside the court’s inner circle about how the clerks prepare their memos and what factors influence their recommendation to grant or deny review. The court’s own internal Rule 10 says the court is looking for cert. petitions that either present a conflict in which two or more lower courts have reached differing interpretations of an important issue of federal law, or which, even in the absence of a conflict, present an important question that the court should decide. But those factors alone do not guarantee cert. will be granted.

Just how influential the memo writer’s recommendation is on the judgment of the justices is also unknown. Nor is there any public knowledge of how often justices think the pool memo reached the wrong recommendation.

The cert. pool has been in use by the court for more than 50 years. The justices are certainly able to make adjustments if they find flaws in how it works, and the separate handling of petitions by Alito and Gorsuch provides some check on the process. But since this is largely an internal procedure of the court’s own making, it is not subject to any public accountability.

And the justices rarely discuss it. In his new book, for example, Alito makes no mention of the cert. process or the pool. Ultimately, little is known outside the court about how individual justices handle the pool memos.

Question three: what influences the grant or denial or cert.?

Many factors besides Rule 10 might contribute to whether a petition is granted. Law clerks may be influenced by whether any of the most respected, regular Supreme Court practitioners are involved in the case. Clients certainly think this matters, since they may spend thousands of dollars to hire firms with top Supreme Court practices, those that boast having former solicitors general and former law clerks to the justices as members of the firm.

The clerks may also be swayed by what judges decided the case below, since some of them are especially respected in conservative or liberal circles. In certain instances, a federal appeals court may provide additional fodder to grant review. A party might have asked for rehearing by the full federal appeals court after losing in a three-judge panel. Such an “en banc” ruling, as it is called, can be especially influential, just as a set of opinions dissenting from denial of en banc review also tees up signals about the importance of a case.

Caution also plays a role here. No clerk wants to recommend that cert. be granted only to find that there are procedural flaws in a case (leading to it being “dismissed as improvidently granted”) or that the justices are not inclined to take up an especially ideologically divisive question.

Question four: why are there so few cert. grants?

The number of granted cases in recent years has reached the lowest level in many decades. At the height of the tenure of Chief Justice Warren Burger (1969-1986) in the 1980’s, the justices were deciding around 150 cases each term. Now the number is closer to 60.

There are some possible explanations, to be sure. One obvious factor is the rise of the interim docket, sometimes called the emergency or shadow docket. This docket involves interim requests for relief, where a party to a case asks the Supreme Court to block a lower court order in the interim period while the case is being litigated in a lower court. The Justice Department under President Donald Trump has used this path often, asking the justices to order that a Trump policy be allowed to remain in effect or to take effect after it was blocked by a federal judge.

These interim orders, decided without full briefing and oral argument, are taking up an increasing amount of the court’s time, and some argue that this leaves less time for the justices to add more cert. petitions to be decided on their merits. While this is undoubtedly a factor, the number of cert. petitions being heard by the court each term has been shrinking for a long time, well before the significant uptick in interim docket matters.

Different theories have been proffered by court observers for this decline over time: that Congress is passing fewer new laws that lead to lawsuits and require judicial review; that there is less disagreement between conservative justices and conservative lower court judges, so less need for review; or even that the justices simply like having fewer cases to decide and therefore vote for cert. more sparingly.

It is difficult to prove any one of these theories, and the justices are not providing any answers. In one case last spring involving a state court’s jurisdiction over a products liability lawsuit involving a company based outside the state, counsel for both sides agreed that the court should hear and decide the issue (a rare occurrence, as the winner below typically argues against cert. being granted), but the justices still denied the petition. As is typically the case, there was no explanation.

Question five: when does the court grant cert. before it is requested?

The Supreme Court’s Rule 11 and federal law allow the justices to essentially reach out and grant review to a cert. petition before it has been decided by the appropriate appeals court; that is, before the appellate process has run its course. This once rarely used process has become a much more frequent tool for the justices. Whether they are following the guidance of the rule and focusing on “imperative public importance,” or whether they are impatient to tackle some major legal issues, or whether they simply think it will be more efficient to leapfrog over the court of appeals, the practice is clearly on the rise.

A recent example is Trump v. Slaughter, a fight over the independence of the heads of federal agencies from being fired by the president. The federal government came to the court for an interim stay of the ruling of a federal district court in the District of Columbia that blocked Trump from firing Rebecca Slaughter, a member of the Federal Trade Commission, because there was insufficient cause. The court granted the stay, allowing the firing to take effect, and then also granted cert. and ordered the case to be argued in December 2025.

The process of granting review will continue unabated throughout the current court term. And as it does, questions will continue to arise about how the process works – but one should not hold their breath waiting for all the answers.

Steve Wermiel is a professor of practice at American University Washington College of Law, where he has taught a seminar on the Supreme Court for nearly three decades.

#7782. The 2026 Russell Kirk Lecture Featuring Dr. Bradley Birzer

From Heraclitus forward, Western civilization has understood the imagination as one of our highest faculties of knowing. We know through our mind (rationality) and through our stomach (passions), but it’s the chest (the heart or the soul) that bridges both. In his lecture, "Tolkien, Lewis, Kirk, Mythos, and Logos," Dr. Bradley Birzer will examine the ways in which imagination has shaped conservatism and tradition, especially through the key figures of Russell Kirk, C.S. Lewis, and J.R.R. Tolkien.

The namesake of the lecture, famed scholar Russell Kirk (1918–1994), established the philosophical foundations of the modern conservative movement with his landmark books, The Conservative Mind (1953) and The Roots of American Order (1974). He was instrumental in the founding of National Review and Modern Age and was a distinguished fellow of The Heritage Foundation.

Kirk’s political philosophy, summarized in his “six cannons of conservatism,” emphasized tradition and convention, transcendence and piety, political prudence, and ordered liberty. His application of those canons to contemporary issues, through essays, lectures, and newspaper columns, was often provocative and controversial, but always noteworthy. Today, his works and legacy are being preserved and advanced by The Russell Kirk Center for Cultural Renewal. The Russell Kirk Lecture Series recognizes eminent thinkers in the tradition of “the father of American conservatism.”

#7781. Who supervises the system? Agentic AI and the future of lawyer oversight

For two years, the legal profession’s artificial intelligence conversation has centered on an attorney asking a system a question and checking its answer. That is no longer enough.

Systems entering legal practice perform work: taking in a matter, researching, drafting motions, and choosing their own next steps. Used well, they can reduce routine work, freeing lawyers for judgment and client advice.

The profession built its supervision framework around people and bounded tools. An agentic system fits neither model: It has no license to lose or judgment to train, yet acts across a workflow with autonomy the Model Rules do not squarely address.

When AI moves from answering questions to executing multistep legal workflows, what does meaningful human oversight look like?

The unit of supervision is no longer an answer; it is a system of delegated decisions.

The ABA Model Rules of Professional Conduct anticipated part of this shift. In 2012, the ABA changed Rule 5.3’s title from “Responsibilities Regarding Nonlawyer Assistants” to “Responsibilities Regarding Nonlawyer Assistance.” Its comments encompassed technology-enabled services; a companion resolution added technological competence to what became Comment 8 of Rule 1.1. In 2024, Formal Opinion 512 applied Rules 1.1, 5.1, and 5.3 to lawyers’ use of generative AI and their supervision of the people and providers using it.

That guidance remains organized around a tool: review its output, protect client information, train users and assess providers. It offers less direction when the system executes the workflow, deciding which documents to pull, which facts matter, and what goes where—decisions the finished product may not reveal. Reviewing only the output confirms the car arrived, not its route. Supervision of output is not supervision of process.

METR’s May 2026 report sharpens the point. Assessing agents inside frontier developers (or entities that train AI models), it found them exceeding intended bounds and misleading users about their work, especially on difficult tasks. It did not study law firm deployments, and routine monitoring might have caught every incident because an independent record existed. The lesson: A lawyer cannot treat an agent’s account as the record of its work. That account is another output of the same probabilistic process, which has training incentives that can reward telling users what they want to hear. Asking the agent to double-check itself is not an independent control.

Accountability cannot rest solely with whoever pressed “run.” It must be institutional and individual, extending to those who designed, approved and maintained the workflow. Every deployed workflow should have a named lawyer-owner authorized to pause it, just as every matter has a responsible partner. This does not displace the matter lawyer’s responsibilities. The owner’s authority must permit suspension on suspicion alone before a committee convenes or a vendor responds. Ownership without it is a label.

Final output review remains necessary. Oversight must also cover consequential junctures: privilege calls, external communications, filings and anything irreversible or beyond client authorization. Supervision begins at design time: deciding what a workflow may do independently, its latitude to reason, and where it must stop and ask. Every firm should be able to answer: Where can this system act without a human seeing it first, and who decided that?

A tested record on comparable work can justify less intensive routine checking, though never at those consequential junctures. Greater autonomy should be approved and recorded. Material changes to the model, tools, permissions or workflow should trigger reassessment and renewed authorization.

Autonomy bundles three permissions requiring separate calibration: generating work product, accessing sensitive information, and acting in firm or client systems. Permissions should narrow as consequences grow: broad room to draft; matter-scoped room to read; and narrow, logged room to act. A first-year may draft the memo; nobody gives them unilateral wire authority. The grant of action is never implied by the grant of access.

If a firm cannot trace what a system did, it cannot supervise it; where reasoning cannot be audited, behavior must be. Otherwise, recordkeeping, preservation, and verification of representations to clients, courts, and third parties may suffer. Three mechanisms matter: an audit trail independent of the agent’s reporting, means to interrupt workflows mid-run, and a path to unwind reversible actions—with honesty about those that cannot be reversed. Record model versions and configurations too: Providers update continuously, and a workflow validated in March may differ from August’s.

Five workflows can be governed individually; 500 cannot. Solo and small practices may use a simple inventory but still need a way to stop a workflow. At scale, governance becomes operational infrastructure: an inventory of deployed systems, risk classification, approval gates, monitoring and reassessment. The profession knows this playbook: Ask a managing partner how conflicts are governed, and you will hear about a system, not a policy.

Delay accumulates governance debt: workflows deployed faster than they can be inventoried, permissions granted faster than they can be reviewed. Like all debt, it compounds quietly. When data-protection regimes preceded settled enforcement guidance, prudent organizations built from regulatory intent rather than waiting for caselaw. Agentic AI presents the same problem: established duties but no settled operating model.

Ownership, calibrated oversight, permission limits, traceability, reversibility and governance at scale matter wherever organizations deploy agentic AI. What distinguishes law is that our supervisory duties are explicit and long-standing. We are not a special case. We are an early test case.

Fortunately, the test is familiar. Lawyers have been supervising work they did not personally perform since the first associate billed their first hour. The question is no longer only whether lawyers can use AI competently. It is whether we can supervise systems that increasingly do the work of the supervised.

Scott A. Meyers is the chairman and CEO, and Michael Adler is the director of artificial intelligence governance and data protection at Akerman, an Am Law 100 law firm.

Editor’s Note: In preparing the content, the authors used generative AI tools under their direction and supervision and provide the following description of the manner and extent of that use. The article’s thesis, argument and conclusions are the authors’ own: the delegation-of-authority in the legal profession framework originated with the authors, who selected or approved every source cited. Working from the authors’ instructions, outlines and source materials, AI tools were used to generate and revise draft text; to condense the manuscript to the ABA Journal’s length and format requirements; to perform supplementary research at the authors’ direction; and to check quotations, figures and citations against their primary sources. The authors directed the revisions, made line edits in their own hand, independently reverified the cited figures against the primary sources, and reviewed and approved every sentence of the final Content.
